A content delivery network solves a simple problem: a single web server sitting in one country cannot quickly serve millions of people scattered across the world. The original copy of a website's files lives on what's called an origin server — the one true source, like a warehouse where every product is first stored. Instead of forcing every visitor to fetch data from that one distant warehouse, a content delivery network places copies of the files on servers scattered across many cities, called edge locations, because they sit at the "edge" of the network, close to where people actually are. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood mini-marts stocking the same popular snacks as a giant central warehouse, so shoppers grab what they need nearby instead of driving across the country for a bag of chips. When a nearby edge location already has the requested file stored and ready, that's called a cache hit — a fast, efficient handoff that avoids bothering the origin server at all. Only when the file is missing locally does a request travel back to the origin, get fetched, and then get stored at that edge location for next time. The result is web pages, videos, and apps that load in a blink rather than a crawl, while also reducing strain on the original source and providing backup if it ever goes offline.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The main storage location holding the original files | It is the ultimate source of truth when nothing else has a copy |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of popular files | It shortens the distance data must travel, speeding things up |
| Cache hit | A successful find of the needed file already stored nearby | It means near-instant delivery with no wasted trip |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Less delay means a smoother, more enjoyable experience |
